Change has been successfully rebased and submitted as 64b85f108ffe3b7b5338974ff7ec6e2b6d92f977

This is going to change the behavior from throwing an exception on initialize() which can be caught, to throwing an exception in the constructor.  This is arguably a good change, but there's a lot of code that needs fixed across a bunch of repos if you want to do this.  I'm in support if that's something you want to make and test, but as-is I don't think we're there.

The commit message makes no mention of the above.  If this is something you've thought about, please comment there.

> This is going to change the behavior from throwing an exception on 
initialize() which can be caught, to throwing an exception in the 
constructor.

I'm not following here, can you kindly explain, which exception is thrown on which line?

Do you mean the `dbus_interface` constructor? I don't see any interesting differences in  exception behavior there but I'm also not an expert on C++ initialization or exceptions.

So i'm looking to you to explain more 😊

> but there's a lot of code that needs fixed across a bunch of repos if you want to do this.

Can you provide one example? I was assuming that for anyone constructing `dbus_interface` it can be done with implicit conversion

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/implicit_conversion.html

> > This is going to change the behavior from throwing an exception on 
> initialize() which can be caught, to throwing an exception in the 
> constructor.
> 
> I'm not following here, can you kindly explain, which exception is thrown on which line?
> 
> Do you mean the `dbus_interface` constructor? I don't see any interesting differences in  exception behavior there but I'm also not an expert on C++ initialization or exceptions.

object_path can throw an exception if the path isn't valid in the passed in string.

So when you call 
```
auto iface = dbus_interface(conn, "//not_a_valid_path", "iface name");
try{
    iface->initialize();
catch(...){
   
}
```

Old code, the exception would be caught.  new code, this would throw to the higher stack.

> 
> So i'm looking to you to explain more 😊
> 
> > but there's a lot of code that needs fixed across a bunch of repos if you want to do this.
> 
> Can you provide one example? I was assuming that for anyone constructing `dbus_interface` it can be done with implicit conversion
> 
> https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/implicit_conversion.html

yeah, you are correct, but the implicit conversion could throw, right?

Thanks for the fast reply 👍

> Fair point.  For some reason I thought there were more checks on construction.

Maybe it's a good thing. If you thought it possible there would be a check and it could throw, maybe it's not that unrealistic to implement that behavior and try it out, see if anything crashes.

> I think I got mixed up on your desire for an "always valid" 
object_path class.  If we agree we're not chasing that anymore, this 
patch seems fine.

I am still preferring the actually-contains-object-path design long-term but it's not what we have currently.

Maybe i will put up a patch for that some other time, but IMO this patch is a lower hanging fruit.

I don't think we are implementing ourselves into a corner with this patch but maybe someone else knows it better.
What is the benefit here if we're not doing any error handling?

What's the benefit here to represent an object path with `std::string` if we already have a value type (`sdbusplus::message::object_path`) for it?


It's inconsistent with the code which is using sdbusplus. Most of that code is using object_path.

`std::string` has quite a large API surface and most of that is not needed when dealing with object paths inside of sdbusplus.

https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/string/basic_string.html

Cleaning up this API can make the code more readable and more robust.

> What's the benefit here to represent an object path with `std::string` if we already have a value type (`sdbusplus::message::object_path`) for it?

Because it exists, and has existed prior to object_path, and has quite a bit of code that we know works.  If we're not adding safety anywhere, why is this interface better?  Is it just that it's an easier to use type?  Why does that matter within the class itself?

> 
> 
> It's inconsistent with the code which is using sdbusplus. Most of that code is using object_path.
> 
> `std::string` has quite a large API surface and most of that is not needed when dealing with object paths inside of sdbusplus.
> 
> https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/string/basic_string.html
> 
> Cleaning up this API can make the code more readable and more robust.

Code more readable, maybe.  More robust, I'm not sure I see how?  Maybe something to add to your commit message?

> If we're not adding safety anywhere,

In your other response you wrote

> object_path can throw an exception if the path isn't valid in the passed in string.

So either using `object_path` gives us exceptions in cases where there were none before (i don't think so), increasing the safety, or, it does not, in which case the change is safe to do and improves readability (intent to pass object path).

> Code more readable, maybe.  More robust, I'm not sure I see how?

If we use a simpler type with less API surface, IMO that makes the code more robust and easier to review / change.

Then we can be more confident that throughout the code only the supported operations are performed on the object path.

We can only be sure of it if the `str` member of `object_path` were private, but one step at a time.

> Because it exists, and has existed prior to object_path,

Yes, a good sign we should change it. Now that we have the `object_path`, we can apply it everywhere we want to represent object paths.

> > If we're not adding safety anywhere,
> 
> In your other response you wrote
> 
> > object_path can throw an exception if the path isn't valid in the passed in string.
> 
> So either using `object_path` gives us exceptions in cases where there were none before (i don't think so), increasing the safety, or, it does not, in which case the change is safe to do and improves readability (intent to pass object path).
>

> 
> If we use a simpler type with less API surface, IMO that makes the code more robust and easier to review / change.
> 
> Then we can be more confident that throughout the code only the supported operations are performed on the object path.
> 
> We can only be sure of it if the `str` member of `object_path` were private, but one step at a time.
> 
> > Because it exists, and has existed prior to object_path,
> 
> Yes, a good sign we should change it. Now that we have the `object_path`, we can apply it everywhere we want to represent object paths.

If we're in agreement that object_path as a class remains "sometimes valid", my above points are moot, and this can go.

If you agree that the "sometimes valid" part of object_path is remaining, then yes, this patch works.
